title: Measuring and Reducing Your Code’s Carbon Footprint
subtitle: Measure energy and carbon intensity before choosing an optimization
summary: Pip speeds up a town report by adding processors. The clock improves; total work does not. Following power, runtime, grid intensity, and equipment across accounting boundaries reveals why speed alone cannot prove lower carbon. Pip profiles the work before deciding what to remove, move, or delay.

concepts.title: Carbon accounting
concepts.body: Pip’s town report uses 2 kWh on electricity rated at 300 g CO2e/kWh: 600 g CO2e for that electricity. Average power and runtime determine energy; supplying electricity’s carbon intensity determines associated emissions. Pip writes the boundary beside the result. Equipment manufacturing is excluded, not magically emission-free.

concepts.title: Scopes of emissions
concepts.body: Pip moves computation to a supplier and celebrates an empty local meter. The town’s accountant stops the party: Scope 1 covers direct emissions, Scope 2 purchased electricity, and Scope 3 other value-chain effects, including manufacturing and device use. Pip redraws the boundary. Moving impact is not necessarily removing it.

steps.text: Pip checks where the impact went.
Scope 3 follows the wider value chain.

concepts.title: Where and when
concepts.body: Pip’s report can wait until morning. A lower-carbon place or period might reduce emissions, but processor use, transfers, user geography, latency, availability, and resilience constrain the move. Pip checks electricity data and the deadline before scheduling. A flexible workload creates a choice; “overnight” alone does not prove cleaner electricity.

steps.text: Flexible work can change time or place.

concepts.title: Profile before optimize
concepts.body: Pip hunts for a clever algorithm; the profile points to verbose logging. The book’s Log.Write example shows why measuring first matters. Pip removes unnecessary log generation and remeasures energy. Faster execution can still use more parallel processors or trigger more traffic: a shorter stopwatch reading is not a carbon measurement.

steps.text: Verify energy instead of trusting wall time.

misconceptions.claim: Carbon accounting is equivalent to ordinary functional correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter separates this concern from “works as coded”: Operational electricity can be converted to carbon dioxide equivalent: energy use depends on average power and runtime, while emissions depend on the carbon intensity of the electricity supplying the location..

misconceptions.claim: A single review proves the product will remain responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Users, contexts, and dependencies change; feedback, monitoring, and revision are required.

scenario.title: Carbon-aware batch processing
scenario.context: Pip’s nightly town report consumes substantial compute. A faster rewrite may add processors; profiling and flexible scheduling offer another route.

options.label: Profile, then schedule flexible work
options.benefit: Targets the largest processor cost and uses cleaner electricity when constraints allow.
options.cost: Migration and delayed results add operational complexity and may affect freshness.
options.consequence: The team removes a logging hotspot and shifts nonurgent work, documenting latency and resilience limits.

options.label: Optimize runtime only
options.benefit: Can return results sooner with familiar code changes.
options.cost: More parallel processors may offset energy savings.
options.consequence: A fast rewrite lowers wall time but raises total compute, prompting a measurement-led correction.

scenario.debrief: Pip profiles waste, then checks scheduling against deadlines and resilience. A runtime improvement needs an energy and emissions check.

quiz.question: Which quantities are used in the chapter’s basic carbon calculation?
options: Number of commits and lines of code
quiz.explanation: Electricity use depends on power and runtime; emissions also depend on the supplying grid’s carbon intensity.

quiz.question: What are Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3?
options: Direct emissions, purchased energy emissions, and other value-chain emissions.
quiz.explanation: The chapter uses the standard scope distinction to broaden accounting.

quiz.question: Why profile before optimizing for carbon?
options: Carbon depends only on programming language.
Measurement identifies the expensive behavior; faster code is not automatically lower carbon.
quiz.explanation: The debugging Log.Write case shows how profiling finds disproportionate work.

exercise.title: Measure carbon

story.title: The report that finished faster but cost more
